sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.markdown: **Vermont credentials chimney sweeping for work in public buildings — see §1a.** For *contracting*, there is only a thin registration. Vermont historically licensed no general/residential contractors; **Act 182 (2021 Adj. Sess., eff. Jul 1, 2022), codified at 26 V.S.A. chapter 106**, created a **Residential Contractor Registration** administered by the Secretary of State's Office of Professional Regulation (OPR). Under **26 V.S.A. § 5501(a)** a person must **register with OPR before contracting with a homeowner to perform residential construction for more than $10,000**; **§ 5509** requires **$1,000,000 per-occurrence / $2,000,000 aggregate liability insurance** and a written contract for work over $10,000 (STATE LAW). **Registration is a registry entry + insurance/disclosure attestation — there is NO exam and no competence test**; chimney sweeping and small repairs of $10,000 or less fall outside it. Public registry: **sos.vermont.gov/residential-contractors**. Regulators told VTDigger in Apr 2026 that few contractors are registered and a bill (H.718) was under discussion; **no enacted change to chapter 106 was found** (statutes online show no amendment since Act 182).

sections.rawHeading: 1a · Sweep Certificate of Fitness (GOV — high confidence; scope resolved Sep 15, 2026)
sections.title: Sweep Certificate of Fitness
sections.markdown:
**The Division of Fire Safety (Dept. of Public Safety) issues a T4 Chimney Sweep Certificate of Fitness (TQP)** for those who "clean, maintain and evaluate chimneys and solid fuel burning appliances" (firesafety.vermont.gov/licensing/t4-chimney-sweep). The rule text is **2025 Vermont Fire & Building Safety Code § 1:1.13.1(5)**: "Sweeping, maintenance and evaluation of Chimneys and Solid Fuel Burning Appliances – A current certificate from the Chimney Safety Institute of America, Certified Chimney Professionals, OR National Chimney Sweep Guild (NCSG) at the Certified Chimney Professional Level. Eight hours of related instruction is required for certificate renewal every three years." (The DFS web page still lists only CSIA or CCP; the rule adds NCSG.) TQP certifications run three years. **Public roster: data.vermont.gov "T4 Certifications" (data.vermont.gov/Government/T4-Certifications/tjh9-m65b).** DFS also issues Gas Certificates of Fitness.

**Scope — who actually has to hold it (RESOLVED from rule + statute text):** the Code states "These rules apply to 'public buildings' as defined by 20 V.S.A. Chapter 173." **20 V.S.A. § 2730** defines public buildings to include rental accommodations, workplaces, offices, hotels, restaurants and similar, and **excludes "an owner-occupied single-family residence, unless used for a purpose described in subsection (a)"** (an owner-occupied home with an ADU is excluded unless the ADU is rented). So **the T4 requirement governs sweep work in public buildings — rentals, multi-family, commercial — and does not legally require a certificate to sweep an owner-occupied single-family home.** A related rule, **§ 1:11.5.1.7.1**, requires fuel-fired heating appliances in covered buildings to be inspected at least once every 2 years by persons certified under § 1.13 — so landlords, not homeowners, carry a recurring certified-inspection duty. *(This scope reading combines the Code's applicability clause with § 2730; DFS has not published a sentence stating it for T4 specifically. Page copy should say "required for work in rentals and other public buildings; not required by state rule for an owner-occupied single-family home — though many sweeps who hold it work in both.")*

Interlock: **26 V.S.A. § 5502(2)(A)** exempts from OPR registration "a tradesperson licensed, registered, or certified by the Department of Public Safety acting within the scope of his or her license, registration, or certification" (and § 5502(2)(B) businesses working primarily through such people) — a certified sweep may lawfully be absent from the SOS registry, so check the DFS roster first.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Narrower than in most states, but not closed. The OPR registry verifies **insurance and identity, not competence**, and jobs of $10,000 or less need no registration. The **T4 certificate writes NCSG-CCP/CCP/CSIA certification into a state credential — but only for work in public buildings.** For an owner-occupied single-family home, the state requires no sweep credential at all, and no Vermont credential tests masonry *repair* competence. An independent audit still adds the layers the state doesn't check for homeowners (cert check, insurance below $10k, photo evidence, review integrity).

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (REF/GOV — SPIR customary, not statutory)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.markdown: Vermont sellers owe a common-law duty not to conceal known material defects. The customary vehicle is the **Seller's Property Information Report (SPIR)**, the Vermont REALTORS form, which names "chimney" and "fireplace" in its structural section and asks heating-system type including wood and pellet (form content per Jul 2026 research). **The SPIR is NOT mandated by statute** — Vermont law does not require sellers to complete it; it is used voluntarily by the industry (REF: Peet Law; Bucknam Law). Statutory disclosures that do exist: **flood-risk disclosure, 27 V.S.A. § 380** (floodready.vermont.gov/disclosure, GOV), groundwater/testing information for homes not on public water, and federal lead-paint disclosure for pre-1978 homes (NATIONAL STANDARD). No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: The **Vermont Consumer Protection Act, 9 V.S.A. chapter 63 (§ 2453 prohibits unfair/deceptive acts)**, gives a private right of action and Attorney General enforcement, with damages and attorney's fees (and exemplary damages available). Home-solicitation sales carry a **3-business-day right to cancel under 9 V.S.A. § 2454 ("Purchase contracts; rescission")** — the consumer may cancel until midnight of the third business day; the seller must tender refunds within 10 days. That is the exact mechanic against chimney scare-sales. Complaints: Vermont AG Consumer Assistance Program (run with UVM).

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: **There is no statewide adopted IRC in Vermont.** The **2025 Vermont Fire & Building Safety Code (effective Nov 5, 2025)**, administered by the Division of Fire Safety, adopts **NFPA 1 (2021), NFPA 101 (2021), the 2021 IBC and 2021 IEBC**, with NFPA 70 (2023) and the 2024 International Plumbing Code; it replaced the 2015 Code (in effect Oct 10, 2016 – Nov 5, 2025). The DFS T4 page states NFPA 211 is adopted. **The Code applies only to public buildings (20 V.S.A. ch. 173)**, so owner-occupied single-family homes are outside the state building/fire code; rentals are inside it. A separate statewide Residential Building Energy Standard applies to homes (30 V.S.A. § 51, edition not re-verified). Some municipalities (e.g., Burlington) adopt and enforce local codes. Chimney relines, rebuilds, and solid-fuel appliance installs are permit/code work in public buildings and in municipalities that enforce locally; for a single-family owner-occupied home in a town without local enforcement there may be no permit process.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — high confidence; strong at sale)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **9 V.S.A. chapter 77.** **§ 2882** requires CO alarms in the vicinity of bedrooms in single-family dwellings (alarms in dwellings constructed after July 1, 2005 powered by building electrical service plus battery). **§ 2883** — the standout — requires that **at closing of the sale of a single-family dwelling the seller certify in writing that the dwelling contains compliant smoke and CO alarms**; if the buyer notifies the seller by certified mail within 10 days after conveyance that an alarm is not operable, the seller must comply within 10 days; noncompliance does not create a title defect. § 2882 does not require an owner-occupant to maintain the devices afterward. Rentals and other public buildings are covered by the Fire & Building Safety Code (e.g., NFPA 101 § 24.3.4.2 placement). A genuine **pre-sale CO obligation** — a natural tie-in to a chimney/stove inspection at transfer.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: Vermont has among the **highest wood/pellet-heat shares in the nation**, so solid-fuel practice carries the content weight. No statewide burn-ban regime; federal EPA new-stove emission standards apply (NATIONAL STANDARD). Some towns regulate outdoor wood boilers — **name the local ordinance per listing town; VERIFY.**

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The Vermont AG's Consumer Assistance Program pursues home-improvement fraud, and the door-knock "we were in the neighborhood / noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook 9 V.S.A. § 2454 home-solicitation problem. VTDigger (Apr 16, 2026) reported regulators believe many contractors operate unregistered. **Specific VT chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT FOUND.** Use pattern language only.

sections.title: Season calendar
sections.markdown: Cold northern-New-England climate; heavy wood heat, long season. Burn season ~Oct–Apr (longer in the Northeast Kingdom/higher elevations). Rush: SEP–NOV. Best booking: APR–JUN.

sections.title: Price seeding (internal)
sections.markdown: Chittenden County (Burlington) and resort towns (Stowe, Manchester) run near/above national; the Northeast Kingdom and rural towns nearer or below national. Regionalize on the Burlington/resort vs rural split.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: **Vermont is the state that checks the sweep — in the buildings the state already regulates — and checks the alarms at sale.** It is the only state found so far that writes NCSG-CCP/CCP/CSIA certification into a state credential, with a downloadable public roster. But the credential lives inside the Fire & Building Safety Code, which covers public buildings; a homeowner in an owner-occupied single-family house gets no state-required sweep credential, no state building code, and a seller disclosure form that is customary rather than required. What the homeowner does get is unusual: **a seller's written certification of CO alarms at closing.** Page headline: "Vermont certifies sweeps for rentals and public buildings — for your own home, check the roster yourself." The roster being open data makes Vermont the cheapest audit in the country.
